Residents interested in the project could be roughly divided into two camps, those upset about parking restrictions and those worried about potential flooding. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has produced an online survey asking residents for input on housing plans for Moraga Canyon. This marks the beginning of public engagement with the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – an initiative that will study all City-owned land in Moraga Canyon with the goal of possible development in the future. “It’s a good opportunity to have Piedmont residents voice their concerns,” said Kevin Jackson, the city’s Planning Director. “We’re trying to move this project forward and engage with the community. It’ll be a stronger plan with greater community engagement.” A mandate by the state of California requires cities to plan additional housing units in their communities to help meet housing needs across the state. The City of Piedmont, though completely built out and with no additional land on which to build housing, was charged with creating plans to accommodate 587 units of new housing, including 257 affordable units by 2031. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan proposes to build 132 units of new housing (60 of which would be for low-income households). SURVEY QUESTIONS Among other things, the survey asks what community members the following: • When you visit Moraga Canyon, how do you and/or your family spend your time there? • What concerns do you have about new housing development in Moraga Canyon? • Would you be interested in living in multifamily housing in Moraga Canyon? Other questions ask citizens to rank the buildings they would like to see in Moraga Canyon based on architectural style with a scale from 1 to 5. The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/MoragaCanyonSurvey and will remain open through October 20th. articles.text: When Officer Jehan Liles joined the Piedmont Police Department, he noticed one thing immediately. “It’s a community where everybody waves,” he said. “I drive around with my windows down in the patrol car and I’m waving to everybody and almost everybody is waving right back.” It’s what he likes most about Piedmont. A Bay Area native, he grew up in Danville where he attended San Ramon Valley High School. “About half of my family is retired military or has served in the military, so for a long time I had an idea of serving others,” he explained. Liles remembers the exact moment that he wanted to become an officer. “The exact moment I would say… was when I was watching a lot of the footage in the George Floyd era, and a little bit pre-George Floyd, of police officers and their interactions with people.” Seeing those videos in the news marked a turning point for him. He felt there was a need for compassionate, community-based policing and that it was something he could do. “I thought, ‘I could probably help people in a law enforcement capacity and make a contribution to my community,’” he said. His decision to apply for a job in Piedmont came on the recommendation of a long-time friend. “[My friend] said, ‘You should New Piedmont police officer Jehan Liles said he enjoys the “small-town, family-oriented” feel of Piedmont. probably apply to this department... this would be a great fit for the type of policing that you would like to do.’” Shortly after, Liles called Police Captain Chris Monahan and put in his application. Liles believes that 21st-century police work is different from previous decades. To him, that means community policing is a must. “It’s really about being able to serve the community in all sorts of ways... basically, being part of the community even though I don’t live in Piedmont.” Liles said he prioritizes getting to know the members of the community and treating everyone he meets fairly. Liles also enjoys the amount of “like-minded” and “family-oriented” people he meets in Piedmont. Liles himself is married and has two daughters. “[My wife and I] graduated from high school together and started dating the summer we graduated,” he said. “Piedmont is a small town. A lot of people are walking. A lot of people are enjoying the parks. It feels very similar to the type of community that I live in. It feels like home for me.” Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission discussed on Wednesday, October 4 the replacement options for the recently removed sequoia tree on the corner of Bellevue and Mountain Avenue. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales was present to provide background information for commission members. “I’m not sure another sequoia is appropriate unfortunately, due to the shifting weather patterns that we have,” said Gonzales. “Greater heat, less fog – that may not be the type of replacement we would look at.” Gonzales added that the City wants to be sure any potential replacement tree would be appropriate for the climate and soil as well as drought tolerant and would have “low water usage.” Questions were also brought by the Park Commission as to the size and scope of the replacement trees the City is considering. “When we replace trees that are so stately, are we looking at trying to bring that scale of tree back into that site or is it just based on the water requirement?” asked Park Commission member Kimberly Moses. Gonzales said that the city was taking the tree’s “stately” elements into consideration while also striving for a “climate-efficient” replacement. The traffic circle that the sequoia was planted in received very little water which could cause problems for future replacements. When asked by Moses if there Photo courtesy of Oakland Public Library Piedmont’s sequoia gigantea was 133 years old at the time of removal this year. was any avenue for citizens to voice their input on the decision of a replacement tree, Gonzales said, “I don’t know that we have a formal process but it seems like a good idea. We usually welcome it.” “If it’s a stately space, we want a stately tree to be there,” affirmed Gonzales. Last month, the City decided to remove the historic sequoia tree from the corner of Bellevue and Mountain Avenue because its “significant lean” endangered local homes and property. This sequoia tree had been in Piedmont since 1890, making it 133 years old at the time of removal.

articles.text: Race down the stretch at East Bay Agency for Children’s 24th annual Gala on November 4th at the Turf Club atop Golden Gate Fields in Berkeley. Guests at The EBAC Classic will take a victory lap for East Bay children and families as they enjoy specialty cocktails and an epicurean dinner paired with Keenan wines, raise their paddles to bid on world-class getaways in the live auction, stock their cellars with cases of premier vintages from the wine raffle, and “get down” with the Git With It Band. New this year will be the broadcast of the “Inf latable Derby,” a race previously filmed on the Golden Gate Fields track with six intrepid EBAC supporters wearing inflatable animal costumes. Gala guests will root for their favorite contestant in what promises to be a hilarious highlight of the evening. This year’s racing venue and theme encourages guests to wear derby styles such as fancy hats and ascots or equestrian attire including jockey colors or riding breeches. For the 24th year, volunteers from the EBAC Auxiliary are planning another epic party. The EBAC Auxiliary began in Piedmont with founders Diane Goetz and Claire Faughnan still involved today. Funds raised support EBAC, a local non-profit who has been meeting the mental health needs of east bay children since 1952. EBAC’s mission is to improve the well-being of children, youth and families by reducing the impact of trauma and social inequities. Gala chair Amanda Lacau Noguera said, “With the future of Golden Gate Fields and the gorgeous Turf Club uncertain, we are thrilled to give our gala guests perhaps one final opportunity to enjoy a night to remember at this landmark venue while raising money to address the current childhood mental health crisis.” For tickets and sponsorship details, see EBAC.org/Gala.

articles.text: Isabella Wire and Eve Tellegen rehearse in the Piedmont High School Advance Acting Class production of The (One Act) Play That Goes Wrong, opening October 19 at the Alan Harvey Theater. The Piedmont High School Advanced Acting class will perform the one act comedy The Play That Goes Wrong from Thursday to Saturday, October 19-21, with two shows on Saturday. The Tony Award-winning play by Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, and Henry Shields is a global masterpiece guaranteed to make everyone laugh until their stomachs hurt. The Cornley Polytechnic Drama Society is producing a classic murder mystery, The Murder at Haversham Manor, but nothing goes according to plan. Come watch the cast try against all odds to make it through to the final curtain call. “This play has been hilarious and fun to rehearse,” says senior Jake Hanke. “I can’t wait to present some of the most well-coordinated chaos I’ve ever been a part of,” added Ben Sachs. The cast on Thursday, October 19, and the 7 p.m. show on Saturday, October 21, includes: Jake Hanke, Sophie Hess, Charlotte Mascola, Ben Sachs, Clio Salzer, Mary Schickedanz, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Isabelle Wire. The cast on Friday, October 20, at 7 p.m. and Saturday at 2 p.m. includes: Jake Hanke, Sophie Hess, Charlotte Mascola, Ella Puckett, Ben Sachs, Xander Schulte-Sasse, Sadie Shoop and Eve Tellegen. The Play That Goes Wrong has won 11 international awards, including an Olivier Award in the UK for Best New Comedy, a Tony Award for Best Set Design, and the Theater Fans Choice Award for Best Play. Initially created in 2012, the play has toured UK, the U.S. and Australia, and was featured on Broadway from 2017 to 2019. Since 2019 it has been playing New World Stages in New York City. The authors have also created The Goes Wrong Show, currently on Amazon Prime, and Peter Pan Goes Wrong, The Christmas Carol Goes Wrong, among other titles. All performances are in the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High School, 800 Magnolia Avenue, Piedmont. General admission tickets are $16 for adults and $6 for students and seniors. Purchase tickets at: https://www. phs-drama.com/. The One-Act Play That Goes Wrong is recommended for audiences age eight and older. articles.text: I recently was asked, “How can I improve creativity in my life if I’m not an artist?” I was delighted by this question because the reality is that most of the time when we are asked to employ our creative minds, it is not in the mode of creating traditional art. There are a few among us who make their livings doing art professionally and a decent number of folks who regularly engage in hobbies that involve art. But all of us solve problems, all of us have to think of new solutions, all of us have to invent new pathways to get to an endpoint. So, how do we strengthen that portion of our creative minds? There are a number of traits that are associated with creative personalities and we can choose to grow and strengthen these parts of ourselves and our children. A few of these traits are: Curiosity, Openness, and Playfulness. If you are looking to grow your curiosity, start with the people you see every day. Pretend you are a journalist and start asking questions. Learn about where they came from, what they enjoyed doing in their childhood, what their favorite movie is and why. See if you can get beneath the surface level questions quickly. We can all ask, “What do you do for a living?” but it takes a truly curious person to ask, “Which of your teachers in high school inspired you to be the person you are today?” Openness is a trait all about accepting that there are multiple options to any potential question or problem. The open person practices divergent thinking, rather than convergent thinking, assuming that the list of solutions is always longer than they can even imagine. To practice openness, think of one thing that you are convinced only has one answer and ask yourself how it is possible that there is a different answer. How is it possible that 1+1 does not in fact, equal 2? You were playful when you were a child. Almost every kid is because that’s how children learn about the world around them. So, if you want to get in touch with your playful one, take some time to really watch your own children, if you have kids under the age of 9. See how they play. Remember your own childhood and ask yourself how you played? Try bringing a tiny bit of play back into your life, even if it’s baby steps, like making a smiley face out of your pees at dinner. Find your play, to find your creative! The more you practice curiosity, openness and playfulness, the easier all three will start to feel and the more you are wiring your mind for creative thoughts. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Speaker, Consultant and Coach. https:// gocreate.zone/
articles.title: Cultivating creative traits

articles.text: Villagers in Mitmebo build enclosures for rabbits. Their sales are an important source of livelihood for local families. I’ve been traveling with my family for as long as I can remember. I love seeing new things, trying new foods, and learning about people and their cultures. This year I had an amazing opportunity to visit a refugee camp called Dzaleka in Lilongwe, Malawi. Together with a project manager of Vijana Africa, a non-profit organization, I spent four days in the refugee camp meeting new people, learning about their lives, and listening to them talk about the problems they face in the camp. On the last day I met with some of the refugee camp beneficiaries who live on the boundary of Dzaleka. While residents of Dzelaka are struggling with dire situations of their own including meeting basic needs and seeking asylum, they also must support their bordering villages who see the refugee camp as an unwelcome neighbor. Community beneficiaries expressed the problems they face with their rabbit and pig farms. Vijana Africa supports 25 widows who are pig and rabbit farmers. The rabbits and pigs provide critical protein for the participants’ families, and a small but important source of income. When a beneficiary sells rabbits, she is able to satisfy some of her family needs. Eighteen of the 25 beneficiaries have been successful in raising rabbits as a regular source of income; the other seven are continuing to improve their farming. While meeting with the beneficiaries I learned that one of their main problems is keeping the rabbits alive and safe. More than 50% of the rabbits are lost due to lack of enclosures. With my resources at home and my experience with Girl Scouts, I quickly realized that I could help Vijana reach their goals. This is when I decided that building rabbit and pig enclosures would be the perfect project for my Gold Award. Over the next nine months I worked remotely with a team of refugees on the ground. We were able to build three large rabbit and pig enclosures in three different villages. Ultimately, I returned to Dzelaka in July to complete the final construction and meet with the refugees and beneficiaries again. I will follow the progress of the project and help with future developments. Julia Montes is a junior at Piedmont High School. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

By Julia Montes I’ve been traveling with my family for as long as I can remember. I love seeing new things, trying new foods, and learning about people and their cultures. This year I had an amazing opportunity to visit a refugee camp called Dzaleka in Lilongwe, Malawi. Together with a project manager of Vijana Africa, a non-profit organization, I spent four days in the refugee camp meeting new people, learning about their lives, and listening to them talk about the problems they face in the camp. On the last day I met with some of the refugee camp beneficiaries who live on the boundary of Dzaleka. While residents of Dzelaka are struggling with dire situations of their own including meeting basic needs and seeking asylum, they also must support their bordering villages who see the refugee camp as an unwelcome neighbor. Community beneficiaries expressed the problems they face with their rabbit and pig farms. Vijana Africa supports 25 widows who are pig and rabbit farmers. The rabbits and pigs provide critical protein for the participants’ families, and a small but important source of income. When a beneficiary sells rabbits, she is able to satisfy some of her family needs. Eighteen of the 25 beneficiaries have been successful in raising rabbits as a regular source of income; the other seven are continuing to improve their farming. While meeting with the beneficiaries I learned that one of their main problems is keeping the rabbits alive and safe. More than 50% of the rabbits are lost due to lack of enclosures. With my resources at home and my experience with Girl Scouts, I quickly realized that I could help Vijana reach their goals. This is when I decided that building rabbit and pig enclosures would be the perfect project for my Gold Award. Over the next nine months I worked remotely with a team of refugees on the ground. We were able to build three large rabbit and pig enclosures in three different villages. Ultimately, I returned to Dzelaka in July to complete the final construction and meet with the refugees and beneficiaries again. I will follow the progress of the project and help with future developments. Julia Montes is a junior at Piedmont High School. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team suffered a devastating 16-13 loss on the road to Alameda on Saturday evening, October 7 at Thompson Field. Though it was Piedmont’s Homecoming game, it was played in Alameda due to Piedmont’s Witter Field being unplayable due to construction. With Piedmont driving to the 1-yard line and the clock ticking down to the final seconds, on a 3rd-and-inches situation, the Highlanders called a dive play for running back Tommy Ashton. Although Ashton appeared to have stretched the ball several inches past the goal line, the referees called the Highlanders’ running back short and the game over. It marks the second straight game in which Piedmont was come out on the wrong end of an official’s decisions. In a game with Arroyo on September 23, receiver Sam Shelby was Photos by Steve Long Tommy Ashton ran for 134 yards on 20 carries against Alameda. He was stopped short of the goal line for the potential game-winning touchdown in a controversial decision by the officials. wrongly ejected in the second quarter by the same official who called Ashton short in Saturday’s game. It’s a situation that has left a sour taste for PHS coach Jordan Seiden. “The clock was going from to Sam Shelby (#2) had seven receptions for 114 yards and a touchdown, including an 80-yard scamper down the sideline. 2 to 1 and Markos handed the ball off to Tommy. You could see on film that Tommy’s body is halfway across the goal line and our entire offensive line is in the end zone with the ball. According to them, we came up an inch short. Piedmont’s tennis team achieved its first two Western Alameda County Conference wins of the season last week, defeating Berkeley 6-1 on Thursday, October 5 at home, and blanking Alameda 7-0 on the road two days earlier. “Everyone continued their good play with the only loss at No. 2 singles against Berkeley. Kate Jumper ran into a very good opponent. We also defeated Alameda 7-0, which is quite the result after beating them 4-3 last year,” said coach Jim Landes. Tanya Kononova continued her strong play at No. 1 singles, beating Berkeley’s Ariana Alharazy and Alameda’s Juliana Johnson in straight sets. Kononova also defeated Johnson in last year’s WACC championship match. “I feel like I’m playing with a lot more control over the ball. It makes me happy,” said Kononova. “I’m not as consistent as I’d like it to be. It’s also about staying mentally composed on the court. But I’ve been able to put more focus on the details and refining the smaller things,” she added. 6-1 over Berkeley Piedmont made quick work of Berkeley with No. 1 doubles team of Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon winning the first match after the Yellowjackets had to forfeit due to an injury while PHS led 3-2 in the first set. From there, Kononova won her match 6-2, 6-0 at No. 1 singles. Maddie Tran and Samantha Huynh then won 6-2, 6-4 at No. 2 doubles, while Inara Mehta and Abigail Call won 6-2, 6-0 at No. 3 to claim Piedmont’s clinching fourth victory. After that, Carolina Romanczuk won in three sets at No. 3 singles, 3-6, 6-3, 6-1. Arianna Kortum then brought in a 6-1, 6-3 win at No. 4 singles. In its match at Alameda on October 3, Kononova rolled to a 6-1, 6-4 victory at No. 1 singles. Jumper, at No.2 singles, had to battle in a three-set match, but came away with a victory, 1-6, 6-1, 7-6 (7-3). At No. 3, Romanczuk won 6-4, 6-1, while Sophie LaForte won 7-6 (7-5), 1-6, 10-8. On doubles, DeFazio and Eisemon won at No. 1 in three sets, 6-4, 2-6, 6-3. Tran and Huynh won 7-5, 6-3 at No. 2, while Ellie Broscow and Mehta paired at No. 3, winning 7-5, 6-1. Photos by Jonathan Comeux Starting on Breakwater Avenue in Hayward, the Hayward Shoreline Interpretive Center starts your trail. The area is known for the old salt farms from the 1850s. Remnants can still be found today, especially at low tide. The Cogswell Marsh was created in 1980 and sustains wildlife native to San Francisco Bay. The trail is entirely flat and gravel, making it a popular area for off-road bikers. We passed 98 people on the 10-mile round trip, so slightly less than 10 people per mile. When factoring that more than 60 of which were on bikes, interactions are minimal and solitude is optimal. The hike begins as you pass the Hayward Interpretive Center on Breakwater Avenue in Hayward. The Center was constructed in in 1985 and is surrounded by 145 acres of fresh and brackish waters. You’ll then reach the Cogswell Marsh, a 250-acre tidal marsh completed in 1980. It’s among the most thriving marshlands of Hayward. The largest is the Ora Loma Marsh, a 364-acre tidal marsh with seasonal wetlands and transitional uplands created in 1997. You can spot various types of birds at all three wetlands, including herons, egrets, sandpipers, common yellowthroats, and black-necked stilts. If wildflowers are more your calling, the marshlands are host to all types of species. East Bay Regional Parks provides a comprehensive list (https://www. ebparks.org/sites/default/files/ ebrpd_hayward_shoreline_wildflowers.pdf) of all the wildflowers at the Hayward Shoreline. articles.text: The 2023 de Young Open has selected three Piedmont artists to display work in the museum galleries – Irene Nelson, Bonnie Bonner, and Emily Keyishian. The exhibit is limited and prestigious. Out of 7,776 applicants, only 883 artists were chosen for the exhibition. For the uninitiated, the de Young Open is a new exhibition focusing on local artists – an exhibit that “takes the pulse of creative energy and culture” in the Bay Area, according to the museum. Hosted every three years by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (FAMFSF), the de Young Open is unique because it is the only major U.S. museum program that is designed for local artists to show their work and is simultaneously free to enter. “I was just thrilled and awestruck,” said Keyishian, one of the selected artists. She is an abstract artist who makes paintings with smooth geometric Irene Nelson is an abstract artist who explores themes of gesture and form through her paintings. Bonnie Bonner explores themes of nature in her eco-sculpture and illustration work, both of which were featured in this year’s Art Walk. Emily Keyishian is an abstract artist whose work focuses on themes of migration and belonging. shapes that drip down the canvas in a multi-colored dreamscape. Many of her pieces are named after songs from music legends like Tom Waits and Miles Davis. “I applied [to the de Young Open] three years ago and I didn’t get in,” added Keyishian. “All of art is kind of about rejection, and you get used to it. It just becomes part of your DNA. So getting that email [of acceptance] …I can’t even articulate how it felt.” Bonnie Bonner had a similar reaction when learning her art had been accepted into the de Young Open. “I was totally surprised,” she said. “I tried to get in three years ago and it was very hard to get in.” Bonner (Joanne Palamountain) has been a local botanical artist for over 20 years. Botanical art is a genre that combines the creativity of traditional fine arts with the added goal of scientific accuracy. Because of how broad its themese can be, Bonner’s work often spans mediums from sculpture to traditional ink and painting. Her piece in this year’s de Young Open is titled “Singed Wildfire,” as a tribute to a close friend who lost all her paintings in the recent California wildfires. “I’m really honored that I was chosen and that my work is part of the show,” said Irene Nelson, whose work was also included in the 2020 de Young Open. Nelson began her art career after a 30-year career in graphic design. For the past 15 years she has been a full-time artist making abstract art inspired by gesture and form that critics have called “emotionally charged but whispering truth.” Nelson currently has a show on display through November 4 at the Manna Gallery, 473 25th Street in downtown Oakland. articles.text: Murakami: Monsterized, the first solo exhibition in San Francisco by Japanese artist Takashi Murakami, is now on view at the San Francisco Asian art Museum. The exhibit, formally titled Takashi Murakami: Unfamiliar People — Swelling of Monsterized Human Ego, will be on display through February 2024. Born in 1962. Murakami is an internationally recognized contemporary artist and major figure in global pop culture. His influences draw from the aesthetic characteristics of the Japanese artistic tradition and postwar Japanese culture. Murakami’s influence in the contemporary art world makes his works highly sought-after in art trades. His vibrant prints maintain a consistently high value. In this exhibition, the artist’s larger-than-life paintings and sculptures use monsters, a common theme in his pieces, as a central motif. Laura W. Allen, Senior Curator of Japanese Art at the Asian, said, “The visual DNA of Murakami’s characters has origins in centuries-old styles in Japanese art, such as depicting Buddhist arhats and Daoist immortals as wizened beings with strange features, bulging eyes, and bared teeth.” Murakami: Monsterized is open until 6 p.m. Friday through Monday and until 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Visit https://www.asianart.org/ to learn more.

articles.text: Angel Adedokun and Jordan Covington in the San Francisco Playhouse production of Nollywood Dreams. San Francisco Playhouse presents Nollywood Dreams, a new comedy by Jocelyn Bioh, playing onstage now through November 11. Set in Lagos, Nigeria in the 1990’s, the play follows Ayamma Okafor, played by Angel Adedokun, who dreams of stardom. She has her heart set for the bright lights of Nollywood, the burgeoning Nigerian film industry akin to California’s Hollywood. She and her sister Dede, played by Brittany Nicole Sims, toil with their parents’ travel agency and unexpectedly audition with Nigeria’s best-known director, where Nollywood Dreams begins to unfold. The playwright hoped to capture a moment in time in Nigeria, one that most Western audiences don’t get to see, and blend it with comedic elements. “That’s an important goal for me. I really am trying to break open people’s singular narrative of Africa and African stories,” Bioh told the San Francisco Chronicle. “We learn about these people who inhabit the continent, and it allows us to have a more humanizing perspective on them.” Directed by Margo Hall, the stage play premiered on October 4. articles.text: San Francisco Opera premieres Lohengrin onstage this Sunday, October 15. The opera, composed by Richard Wagner, follows the story of noblewoman Elsa who faces charges of murder in the disappearance of her brother Gottfried, heir to the duchy of Brabant. King Heinrich, in Brabant to raise an army, calls on Friedrich von Telramund to explain why the country is torn apart. Telramund claims that Elsa, daughter of the late Brabantian ruler, has murdered her brother. The climax comes when a mysterious knight appears to defend Elsa’s honor on the condition that she marry him without knowing his name. Music Director Eun Sun Kim brings Wagner’s opera to life, with a well-rounded cast including Simon O’Neill as Longhengrin, Julie Adams as Elsa, Kristinn Sigmundsson as the king, and Brian Mulligan as Friedrich von Telramund. The opera also stars Judit Kutasi and Thomas Lehman in their San Francisco Opera debuts. The production is directed by David Alden, with Paul Steinberg as set designer and Gideon Davey as costume designer. Performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House on October 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, and November 1. Visit an hour before performances for a 20-minute overview of the opera. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet will join other leading dance companies to celebrate the 10th anniversary of World Ballet Day on November 1. It will be part of a group of dance companies, including The Royal Ballet and The Australian Ballet. More than 60 companies from across the globe will have a 24-hour celebration of ballet and dance. The event will be streamed on YouTube and Facebook. Over the course of the day audiences can tune in to see classes, rehearsals, and other exclusive footage of the world’s ballet stars and performers. “As the oldest professional ballet company in the United States, we’re honored to partner with The Royal Ballet and The Australian Ballet in this global celebration and the tenth anniversary of World Ballet Day,” said Tamara Rojo, San Francisco Ballet’s new Artistic Director. “We’re delighted to be able to give viewers glimpses of the creative processes in real time, and honor ballet as a living art and universal language.” Other featured ballet companies include the Korean National Ballet, Hong Kong Ballet, Cape Town City Ballet, Finnish National Ballet, Singapore Ballet, and San Francisco-based Smuin Ballet. The season-opening concert on November 4 is presented as part of the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music. The program will include Berlioz’s Roman Carnival Overture, Cavaterra’s Rhapsody On A Windy Night, and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4 in F minor Op. 36. This year YPSO celebrates its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director/Conductor. He will be conducting 99 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from Bay Area cities as far north as Napa and as far south as Pleasanton. YPSO has a very full-activity calendar this season – they are performing four concerts, participating in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, the playing at the Bay Area Youth Orchestra Festival at Davies Symphony Hall, and embarking on a 9-day, 3-concert summer tour to Japan in June 2024. About California Festival YPSO is one of 95 organizations participating in the California Festival: A Celebration of New Music, (cafestival.org) presenting some of the most innovative and compelling music from around the world for two weeks, November 3-19, 2023, in venues throughout the state. Announced in January 2023 and conceived by Los Angeles Artistic Director Gustavo Dudamel, San Diego Symphony Music Director Rafael Payare, and San Francisco Symphony Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen, the California Festival highlights the collaborative and innovative spirit that thrives in California by inviting musical organizations of all kinds to incorporate works written within the past five years into their broader season programs. articles.text: There are some life experiences from which there is no recovery. No matter how often the word “closure” is offered as an outcome, in truth, closure is a myth when parents lose a child. The only question is how those who face such tragedy endure. That is the essence of Rabbit Hole. The film begins with Howie (Aaron Eckhart) and Becca (Nicole Kidman) Corbett clinging to their routines while they cope with a canyon of distance that exists between them. The tension is palpable. Only gradually is it revealed that the source of their pain – the spare conversations, the brittle quality to their relationship – is the loss of their 4-year-old son eight months prior. He chased their dog into the street and was hit by a car. The performances of both Kidman and Eckhart are brilliantly crafted. Each copes with a grief that seems insurmountable in a completely different way. They are barely able to function as individuals while navigating the emotional wreckage that has become their lives. Rabbit Hole is never maudlin and never attempts to be melodramatic. It is instead a window without distortion. Audiences may shy away from this film for that very reason, but know that the narrative is rich with fine performances. Diane Wiest as Becca’s mother, who has also lost a son, is exceptional. Sandra Oh’s portrayal of a woman who has found help in a support group but is afraid to leave, is subtle and inspired. The film is adapted from the 2006 Pulitzer Prize and Tony-winning play of the same name, written by David Lindsay-Abaire. Kidman was nominated for an Oscar for Best Actress in a Leading Role. articles.text: Reese Witherspoon and Paul Rudd in How Do You Know How Do You Know is another romantic comedy, the genre du jour. The difference is this comedy was written by James L. Brooks, a veteran Hollywood writer for television and film who is known for snappy dialogue and comedic plots. So, does How Do You Know measure up? The ensemble does a fine job and are easy to watch. First there’s Lisa (Reese Witherspoon), a young woman who has spent her life perfecting her athletic ability (she is a Team USA softball player) and then abruptly, at 31, she’s cut from the team and finds herself a bit lost and at loose ends. When she faces this existential moment, the movie showed real promise. Athletes spend their lives on the field of play, preparing to play a game well, to compete, to run or row or cycle. Because sports are unforgiving, age and the ability of the body to renew declines, and for most athletes time becomes the sword of Damocles. But because this is a comedy and not a serious personal exploration, Lisa hooks up with pro pitcher, Matty (Own Wilson) and finds a diversion in the relationship, ignoring (a sprinkling of denial) that she is living with a well-paid, albeit charming man-child. At one point, frustrated, she looks at Matty and says, “Grow up!” His rejoinder is, “No!” But then Lisa has little faith in marriage or long-term relationships, convinced that couples who have been together for years, have kids and lead a conventional life, are pretending if they seem happy. All of this is somewhat interesting, and then along comes George (Paul Rudd), a mid-level executive, working for his father, Charles (Jack Nicholson). George also happens to be the target of a securities fraud investigation. That’s the setup. Is it charming, even funny? Well, it’s pleasant, with fine performances. Does Brooks display his nicely honed wit? On occasion. He does manage to insert lines such as, “Figure out what you want in life and learn how to ask for it.” Or, “We’re just one small adjustment away from making our lives work.” While both admonitions sound profound in the context of the movie, they also seem nonsensical and mean little. Notice also that the title, How Do You Know, is not posed as a question. The interrogatory is thrown out there by Matty to a group of ballplayers who haven’t a clue and respond with an answer that detracts, for a moment, from what is otherwise a charming movie. articles.text: Making full disclosure, I admit to loving westerns. A durable favorite is Open Range with Kevin Costner and Robert Duvall. But, I acknowledge that I’m pretty promiscuous when it comes to this genre. Westerns are, in their own special way, mythic, even iconic, no matter that they are filtered through the imaginations of novelists and screenwriters and often scrubbed of their burrs and harsh realities. One of my archival favorites will always be The Searchers with John Wayne, Ward Bond, Jeffrey Hunter and Natalie Wood. It was quintessential Wayne who was so good in so many films. Wayne doing Wayne. If I squint a bit, I can even convince myself that The Quiet Man is maybe an Irish western with hearty brogues, hounds tooth jackets, and the lovely, lush Innisfree, Ward Bond as the village priest, and the lovely Maureen O’Hara in a white apron and a simmering temper. Truly wonderful. So, here come the Coen brothers who took a great book by Charles Portis and made it their own True Grit, asking Jeff Bridges to do the heavy lifting as Rooster Cogburn, a dissolute marshal hired by spitfire, Mattie Ross, played perfectly by newcomer Hallee Steinfeld. It’s a great western. A great story, filled with interesting characters, the look of it having a certain patina, which will always be the quirky, ominous signature of Ethan and Joel Coen. The film follows the book closely, hence the eccentric language and formalized sentence structure that is both interesting and at times sharply funny. The actual plot is really immaterial, at least for purposes of this review. Suffice it to say that it’s a kind of road trip with willful Mattie Ross – who actually possesses true grit (or, in the vernacular of the day, sand) – pushing Marshal Cogburn hard into the Indian Territory to track down Tom Chaney, the man who killed her father. Mattie is at the center of the film and in every way special. She’s 14-years-old, hair parted severely, long braids, a remarkable gift of gab, hails from Yell County, Ark., and arrives in Fort Smith alone to settle her father’s affairs. She’s someone to be reckoned with. There is a glorious scene wherein she bargains with a horse dealer, Col. Stonehill, played by character actor Dakin Mathews, that is a treat to watch. True Grit is exceptional, if you appreciate the genre. Do not expect a remake of the Coen’s No Country For Old Men with its cruel, hard edges. This is a completely different movie, better for it. articles.text: I always look forward to tasting the new releases from Ridge Vineyards. In the fall each year they release their wonderful Lytton Springs blend as well as their well-regarded Montebello Chardonnay in addition to a couple of surprises. Ridge Winery has two main facilities. One is a spectacular location on a high ridge (hence the name) overlooking Silicon Valley. You keep climbing this steep road and you never think you ae going to get there and suddenly there it is – with a magnificent view. It’s hard to believe what caused the early Italian pioneers who planted these vineyards so long ago to undertake the effort. This is the home of the Montebello Vineyard, the source of Ridge’s iconic Chardonnay and award-winning Cabernet Sauvignon. The Ridge Montebello Cabernet was in the original Paris tasting of 1976 that knocked the French off the world wine throne. To this day it is one of the world’s most highly rated Cabernets. Their other facility is located on Lytton Springs Rd. just east of Hwy. 101 in Sonoma County. The winery is surrounded by nearly hundred-year-old Zinfandel vines that look like gnarled bonsai trees. This is the home of the Lytton Springs and Geyserville blends as well as many small single vineyard Zinfandels. It is also home to the great former York Creek Petite Sirah (rest in peace) and the dynamic Lytton Estate Petite Sirah – one of the greatest values in California wine. If you are interested in Ridge wines, be sure to check out their website where they have over 100 wines for sale. The wine tasting area at Ridge Lytton Springs.

Wednesday, October 11, 2023 23 By Will Adams Another important visual element of our built environment is signage. It is in many ways a lot like lighting, discussed in the last column. Both tend to stand out when done poorly and unrelated to their context. When designed well, both lighting and signage seem to go unnoticed as they appear to fit right in, as if there were no other way they could have been designed. Besides providing necessary information to people on foot or in cars, appropriate signage can enhance and complement the Signage architecture of a building or landscape of which it is a part. Walking around Piedmont, it is clear that the sensitive and understated use of signs pretty much everywhere contributes to the charm of the city. Like lighting, signage has both a functional requirement and an aesthetic character. Function is of course the first consideration: what is the sign’s purpose? And to whom is it addressed? Clearly there is a huge difference in sign requirements for people walking around town versus those driving cars at various speeds. Unfortunately, often the size and use or purpose of signage is confused. What is appropriate and exciting for Las Vegas or Times Square for example is neither appropriate nor necessary for pretty much anyplace else of less density or of smaller scale. The common signage mistake of using large retail advertising methods when only subtle information is required is not a problem we have in Piedmont. Signage should be designed to fit with the surrounding architectural character, because both in fact work together to orient visitors and let them know where they Four examples of building signage (above): all different, simple, understated, and designed to complement the architecture of which they are a part. This kind of variety adds interest and texture to the city without distracting or overwhelming. These examples, especially the Piedmont Community Church portal and sign, also fall into the “urban design” category, with which readers of this column are familiar. are and where they are headed. When approaching City Hall, for example, unfamiliar visitors, seeing the size of the building cluster, the associated communication towers, and then the landscaping and fountain, have a good idea long before they are sure that this is indeed a civic building. At the final destination, the rather small sign is only a final confirmation that the supposition was correct. A great sign. It is the right size for easy reading of the information without being too big and distracting, and the perfect color for its placement in the parks. Although a regulatory sign, I find it friendly. Photos by Will Adams The specific purpose of a sign and the people to whom it is directed should determine the design: the location, size, shape, text, images, and colors. There are usually numerous good alternatives. Signage is often lighted. Internally illuminated signage has been done badly so often it is prohibited in many places because it is often coarse and annoying. Externally illuminated signage generally has a better opportunity for aesthetic success, provided that the signage is appropriate for the genre of architecture/site/ environs and it is not over lit. In some cities, very strict design review requirements for signs are problematic as they have resulted in a completely uniform, bland, lifeless array of signs, which are ironically hard to interpret or to decipher the required information. In my opinion, the best signs are those that are creative but restrained, and also reasonably varied. These seem to add life, interest, and texture to the street and neighborhood. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 13, 2021. The historical “informational” signs placed throughout the Piedmont Park area are perfect: unobtrusive yet easy to find and read, informative and well designed. They were created for the City’s Centennial in 2007, with support from Piedmont Beautification Foundation, Piedmont Garden Club, Piedmont Historical Society, and the Bechtel Foundation.

articles.text: Thomas Young Kincaid, a 5th generation Piedmonter passed away peacefully at his home in Sparks, Nevada on September 23, 2023 with his loved ones by his side. He was 69. Tom was born in Oakland in 1954 and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1972. Tom retired to Sparks after many years working as the Division HR Manager for Golden State Overnight as well as the Security Lead for Aramark Sports & Entertainment at the Oakland Coliseum. He also worked as a police officer for the Oakland Housing Authority and as a Reserve officer for the Piedmont Police Department. One of his first jobs was as a Regional Training Coordinator for Greyhound Lines in Oakland. Tom is predeceased by his parents Donald H Kincaid and Gaye Lenahan and his beloved dog Brownie. articles.text: A record turnout of 22 readers of the First Mondays Reading Group came to the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on a beautiful, warm day in early fall on October 2. On hand were: Dick Carter, Bob Hall, Bella Almanzan, Ken Young, Darby Gragg, Gerry Gragg, Hillary Honore, Martin Levy, Mike Henn, Adrienne Hamlin, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, June Cohen, Lois Price, Rich Seigel, Dale Benveniste, Carol Warren, Carol Long, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The subject of discussion was The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid, the 2006 memoir by best-selling travel writer Bill Bryson. It was a fun, summertime kind of book and the memoir of the childhood of the author. The group had previously read and discussed Bryson’s The Body: A Guide for Occupants Bryson’s 2019 book of popular science. In The Life and Times he tells of his youth growing up during the 1950s in Des Moines, Iowa. The book’s title comes from an imaginary identity Bryson created for himself, who had the ability to vaporize problem people with his heat vision. Bryson recalls many things that he invented through his imagination: frozen dinners, atomic toilets, and television. His middle class American lifestyle is present throughout the book, Bryson tells amusing stories of his misadventures, and the trouble he and his friends got into, which was common for the Thunderbolt Kid. At the book’s end, Bryson tells readers that “life moves on,” and he wishes the world could be more like life in the 1950s and 1960s. Almost everyone in the group enjoyed the book. Parts of it are can’t-stop-laughing funny, and the stories brought back childhood memories and some nostalgia for the readers. The group talked about 19 cent loaves of bread, kids spending all their time outside, front doors that were never locked, and getting BB guns at age 12, How much the world has changed is staggering. The readers questioned what has been lost versus what has been gained over the last 70 years. The constraints on women’s opportunities and the discrimination experienced by minorities are less today. Life was certainly not as wonderful for everyone as it was for Bryson’s white, middle class family. However, it seems life was a happier and more carefree than it is today. The group was pleased that Jennifer Peltzer brought Nancy Odette. Nanda Parte from India had come for a wedding and joined the walkers. Lisa Leonard and Kris Keller with K-9 best friends Lucky and Rascal were also part of the weekly walk. A strong turnout of 46 walkers and four K-9 best friends arrived at the Exedra for a walk on October 4 as part of the Walking on Wednesdays group. One street that the group hadn’t walked and an early Piedmont land developer they hadn’t talked about this year was Sharon Avenue and William Sharon. The long stretch of Wildwood Avenue between Highland and Crocker Avenues with the leaves turning red on both sides of the street provided a colorful walk. The walkers went to Lincoln Avenue and over to Sheridan Avenue. Going up Caperton Avenue to Mountain Avenue provided some uphill exercise. At Mountain, they went to Sharon Avenue where its history was shared. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi had told of William E. Sharon, his family, and estate in a past issue of the society’s publication. Sharon was born in 1852 and grew up on an Ohio farm. In 1872, he went to San Francisco and then Virginia City, Nevada to work for his uncle, who was a successful banker and silver mine owner. Sharon married Lillian Mygatt in 1876 and became successful in finance and mining too. He was elected to the Nevada State Senate in the 1880s. The Sharons initially lived in Virginia City, but they wanted their children to attend better schools and bought a home in Oakland in 1890. Three years later they purchased nine acres in the Piedmont hills on Mountain Avenue. They built a magnificent three-story house in the middle of their land and called it Casa Montana. With seven children, Lillian’s mother, a housekeeper, cook, and gardener they moved into it in 1898. However, in 1914 the City of Piedmont, then seven years old, imposed a new property tax based on the size of the property, and the Sharons’ taxes increased dramatically. In 1915, the Sharons subdivided their land in a development they called Sharon Terrace. It had 20 lots with frontages on Mountain, Sharon, Dormidera, and Pacific Avenues. Some family members built homes there, and the driveway to Casa Montana became Sharon Avenue. Sharon died at his home in 1926, but Casa Montana continued as a family home. Lillian lived in it until 1934 when she moved into a residential Oakland hotel. Developer George Windsor purchased the remaining land and built his own home at 11 Sharon Avenue and the house at 7 Sharon on spec. He later built homes at 40 and 44 Sharon. Sadly, in 1936 Windsor demolished Casa Montana and replaced it with three homes – 27, 33, and 37 Sharon Avenue. Today, only three Sharon family members’ houses remain from the Casa Montana property – 235 Mountain, 56 Sharon and 52 Sharon Avenue. The walkers continued down to Dormidera Avenue and went to where it intersects with Sharon Avenue. They took a side trip to Sharon Court, which was not part of the original development. For the return walk to the center of town, they had an opportunity to take a somewhat hidden path from Mountain to Sierra Avenue and get back to the city center before the temperature rose to 80 degrees.
